principle: Pick the target player first, then set how much risk to allow
why: Sakurai's theory is that as you increase game essence, you reduce a game's broad appeal. He made the first Kirby deliberately simpler to reach newcomers, slowed Brawl for a casual Wii audience, and went the other way with Kid Icarus: Uprising because casual players were already served. Who you target should follow from the game's design and concept, and there is no one right answer.
how_to_apply: Write down the target player in terms of experience ('beginners', not 'children'), decide how much push and pull they want, then set the risk dials to match. If you go hardcore, make it an explicit goal rather than the default.
anti_pattern: Tuning risk to your own skill; assuming more depth is always better for everyone; defining the audience by age or gender instead of experience.
example: Kirby's Dream Land vs. Super Mario Bros. Melee's speed was harsh on new players and even gave some players tendinitis, so Brawl was slowed. Kid Icarus: Uprising targeted hardcore players because Touch! Generations already covered casual ones. Sakurai suspects 'super casual' players who find even Dream Land too hard are a huge opportunity.
review_question: Who exactly is this for, in experience terms, and does the risk level match them?
keywords: target audience broad appeal accessibility casual hardcore beginners experience level difficulty target market

principle: Be kind to beginners: neutralize threats early and forgive small slips
why: A minor risk to an experienced player can be a massive brick wall to a newcomer. Being hit or missing a jump is a small mistake, so losing a life for it is too harsh. It is hard enough to get people to play at all, and a beginner who gets crushed before understanding the game will quit.
how_to_apply: Give beginners ways to stop threats while the risk is still low, a forgiving health pool, an escape from the steepest penalties, big targets that near-misses still hit, and an opening window where deaths cost little. Keep some penalty for real failure. In competitive play, let newcomers act and have fun before they get flattened.
anti_pattern: One-hit deaths, heavy control inertia or instant death for a missed jump in a game for newcomers; wiping every power-up on death; crushing someone who just came to try the game.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale stops enemies early, the spit attack outranges the inhale, Kirby takes up to six hits and can fly over pits (falling still costs a life), and Whispy Woods is huge. Space Harrier's 'trial time'. Gradius's power-up reset makes players want to quit. Sakurai crushing a couple trying The King of Fighters '95.
review_question: What happens to a first-time player in their first five minutes?
keywords: beginners newcomers kindness forgiving onboarding penalty harshness health flight assist first time player

principle: Never let a player get permanently stuck
why: No matter how fun tense challenges are, the moment players give up, the challenge is worthless. In RPGs you can always level up, but in action games getting stronger won't win, and everyone has a breaking point. Games that force a restart because difficulty can't be changed mid-game have a fundamental design flaw, and an impossible spike after dozens of hours is to be avoided at all costs.
how_to_apply: Let players change difficulty at any time without losing progress. After repeated failures in one spot, offer an easier setting or a skip that counts as cleared, worded so it doesn't humiliate. Provide a floor that is nearly guaranteed to win. If a shipped game proves too hard, patch in an easier option. Teach newcomers explicitly how to turn difficulty down.
anti_pattern: Difficulty locked at the start; an impossible final spike; leaving the easy end of a difficulty system unexplained.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Intensity 0.0 is nearly invincible, but players weren't told clearly that going below 2.0 lowers difficulty. Smash Ultimate's patch made Challenger fights easier and added Very Easy to World of Light. The Last of Us Part I's assists.
review_question: If a player fails the same spot ten times, what does the game offer them?
keywords: stuck difficulty settings change anytime skip stage easy mode assist dynamic difficulty breaking point accessibility

principle: Don't tune difficulty to your team; handicap yourself, then go easier
why: Developers know the game inside and out, so tuning to the best player on staff, or even the median one, leaves it too hard for players who won't spend all their time on your game. What keeps players going isn't other games being hard or you being able to scrape by in your own.
how_to_apply: Tune while handicapped: play one-handed, with lower health or stricter conditions, and make sure you can still clear it. Set difficulty a good deal below what feels right to the team, then lower it once more. Bring in people who have never played and use each one fresh only once; watch children play rather than asking them questions.
anti_pattern: Balancing around the most skilled staff member; calling the same outside tester back as if they were still fresh.
example: Sakurai plays with one hand when balancing. Elementary school play testers who came with friends and snacks.
review_question: Who set this difficulty, how well do they know the game, and were they handicapped?
keywords: playtesting difficulty tuning developer skill bias one-handed handicap fresh testers easier than you think curse of knowledge

principle: Get players back in control within seconds of failing
why: Interest cools fast between the moment the player thinks 'Ugh, I blew it!' and the moment they regain control, and quick retries raise tolerance for difficulty and hardship. The game moving on its own isn't enough; players need to be in control.
how_to_apply: Measure death-to-control time and cut it: a flashy, impactful failure effect of about a second, short loads, no non-interactive screens (if text must remain, let button presses advance it). Make sure enemies can't hit players the moment they respawn, but don't make respawning so free that the game feels mindless.
anti_pattern: Long death sequences, slow fades and loading before a retry; respawning into enemy fire; infinite respawns exactly where you died.
example: No specific title; he states it as a general rule. In competitive FPS play, quick restarts sweep away disappointment.
review_question: How many seconds pass between 'Ugh, I blew it!' and the player's next input?
keywords: retry respawn restart death time load times player time failure loop quick retry checkpoint

principle: Keep every option's peaks and valleys; never average them out
why: Balancing purely on strength trims advantages and patches weaknesses until every fighter is average, and average isn't fun. The more alike options become, the more they feel like the same character and the whole game turns bland. Divisive differences are healthy: you want players to say 'Then let's settle it in a match!'
how_to_apply: When something is too strong, first exaggerate its weaknesses instead of cutting its signature strength, and don't soften weaknesses in the same patch. Reject proposals that make a character more average. Push interchangeable options apart. This applies to move sets in non-competitive games too.
anti_pattern: Shaving strengths and filling in weaknesses until options feel alike; relying on mirror matches to dodge balance problems; backing away from distinctive designs because of social-media bias.
example: Smash Bros. tuning: Sakurai tells the team to keep fighters unique by amplifying shortcomings to offset advantages. Mario vs. Mario has no balance issues but limited push and pull. Fighters differ in movement speed, vulnerability and animation flair.
review_question: After this balance change, does every option still have a clear strength and a clear weakness?
keywords: character balance peaks and valleys uniqueness individuality asymmetry nerf buff roster homogenization mediocre average

principle: Fix balance with the narrowest change that keeps the signature intact
why: One attack has many components (power, speed, duration, windup, follow-through, range, hit size, animation speed, knockback, combo ability, shield damage, shield recovery), so it can be weakened without erasing what makes it special. Kirby's flight got too strong on the NES, and changing its context worked better than cutting it. After launch, touching core systems forces wide re-testing.
how_to_apply: List the move's parameters, mark the defining one, and change a secondary one instead: lengthen the vulnerable follow-through or shrink the hitbox. For an overpowered ability, try shrinking the play space, confining key fights to one screen or lowering its speed before removing it. Post-launch, adjust specific encounters or add an easier option rather than rewriting core AI.
anti_pattern: Flattening the stat that defines a move; cutting a signature mechanic outright; rewriting core AI or global difficulty in a late patch.
example: Smash: keep a move's attack power, lengthen its follow-through. Kirby's Adventure: a bigger info panel, single-screen mid-boss fights and slower flight. Smash Ultimate's narrow difficulty patch.
review_question: Is this fix touching the one thing players love about the option?
keywords: nerf adjustment parameters follow-through hitbox frame data rebalance context patch narrow fix signature mechanic

principle: Scale every penalty and reward to how good or bad the action was
why: Players are happiest when their behavior is compensated correctly, and each success and failure deserves a fitting consequence. A big penalty for a really bad choice can be fun, but you must ask whether the player can ever redeem themselves. Small slips deserve small costs, and failure should still cost something or respawning feels mindless.
how_to_apply: For every reward, penalty and damage value ask how good or bad the triggering action really was. Give irreversible choices an explicit recovery path and cost. Check whether a death that costs the player their build still leaves a realistic way back. Keep the mapping loose enough to surprise: polish out only what feels unreasonable.
anti_pattern: Permanent penalties decided only by scenario logic; a late death that leaves the player hopelessly underpowered; removing party members along with the gear invested in them; rationalizing every reward until the game is predictable.
example: Smash: slow smash attacks earn more damage and knockback than quick neutral attacks. Gradius: arriving late in the game with only a Double after losing power-ups. Score games paying more for stronger enemies.
review_question: Does this consequence match how good or bad the action really was, and is there a way back?
keywords: penalty fairness consequences punishment reward proportion redemption recovery irreversible choice death penalty

principle: Shape difficulty like a mountain trail, not a steady ramp
why: Keeping player and enemy strength in direct proportion makes progress a steady incline, which is a chore: it's just work. Real climbs have peaks to overcome and flat stretches to breeze through. Enemies that scale with the player remove any incentive to get ahead, and growth stages that dip in power create walls.
how_to_apply: Plot player power against enemy difficulty across the game and reshape it into deliberate peaks (bosses that demand a strategy) and flats (unexpectedly empty areas, spots to rack up gains). Don't level-scale enemies to the player. Check every growth stage for dips. Playtest the endgame for spikes.
anti_pattern: A straight diagonal of player and enemy strength; level scaling; an impossible spike at the very end.
example: The mountain-climbing analogy. Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking: care taken so growth stages don't hit a wall in battle.
review_question: Where are the peaks and the flat stretches on your difficulty curve?
keywords: difficulty curve pacing level scaling progression power curve peaks valleys breathers grind rpg balance

principle: If failure means repetition, give players a reason to push on
why: Most players won't enjoy repeating the same content forever; they continue because they want to see what comes next. If more players than expected hit a wall, they may see the same scenery again and again and quit. Dark Souls' pull partly rests on trust in its developer, which a copy doesn't inherit.
how_to_apply: For each likely failure point, list what players will replay on the way back, then shorten it or vary it (randomized equipment, items, events). Make the next area, story beat or reward visible or hinted. If you borrow permadeath or Souls-like systems, write down your own reason to push on.
anti_pattern: Mimicking hard-game systems without creating the pull; low-variety content players must repeat many times.
example: Roguelikes and roguelites vary each run after a defeat. Dark Souls players push on to reach what's next.
review_question: What does a player see on their tenth attempt at this section, and why would they want to keep going?
keywords: roguelike permadeath repetition retries motivation variety souls-like difficult games start over

principle: Layer optional depth over a simple core both audiences can use
why: In a mature market with few beginners, Kirby's Adventure had to satisfy both groups: novices can finish by inhaling and spitting, veterans dig into copy abilities. Making Ryu's full-command shoryuken essential would have split Smash players into those who can and can't do it. Shortcuts only experts use narrow a UI's appeal.
how_to_apply: Build a minimal core that can finish the game or compete, add depth on top, and verify a core-only playthrough works. Offer a one-button version of special inputs and give the full version a modest bonus (a bit more damage or invincibility). Keep novice extras optional and skippable.
anti_pattern: Requiring the depth system to progress; balancing so a hard input is needed to compete.
example: Kirby's Adventure copy abilities and optional one-button minigames on the map. Smash Bros. Ryu: one-button or command shoryuken. Kirby made for beginners but with enough 'oomph' that advanced players enjoy the controls.
review_question: Can someone using only the simplest controls finish or hold their own?
keywords: beginners and experts layered depth optional mechanics skill ceiling skill floor simple inputs command inputs accessibility

principle: Size complexity to your audience and lifespan; hold back what they can't feel
why: You can always add rules to boost push and pull, but overcomplicated rulesets are hard to grasp, so sometimes you must hold back. A game meant to last hundreds of matches still needs a certain level of complexity, but moves too hard to perform hide the push and pull. Constant risk made Kid Icarus: Uprising feel too hardcore, and Melee's speed was harsh on newcomers.
how_to_apply: Decide whether the game is for casual sessions or hundreds of matches and size its depth to match. Before adding a rule, check your target players could still grasp the game. Keep inputs easy enough to feel the push and pull, and lower speed and input density for casual audiences or laggy online play. Keep weakness and combo systems simple in casual games.
anti_pattern: Piling on rules for depth until the game is hard to understand; inputs so hard players cannot feel the push and pull.
example: The original Street Fighter (moves too hard) vs. Street Fighter II. Super Smash Bros. Brawl's slower speed. Kid Icarus: Uprising's land stages, too big and full of enemies with no respawn where you died.
review_question: Would your target player still understand the game after this rule is added?
keywords: complexity depth clarity learning curve casual competitive lifespan input density game speed rules bloat hold back

principle: Tune risk through explicit dials, not a vague difficulty knob
why: In Space Invaders the cannon's width is key to game balance because it determines how great your risk is; it is more than visual design. Kirby's approachability comes from specific dials: inhale range, six hits of health, flight, low inertia. Risk can also move between layers: easy dungeon exits can be offset by harder battles.
how_to_apply: List your risk dials (player hitbox size, partial cover, threat-neutralizing range, hits the player can take, escape tools, control inertia, game speed, target size, enemy durability, how freely players can leave) and set each deliberately. When you lower risk in one layer, decide whether to add it back in another.
anti_pattern: Treating character or hitbox size as purely visual; removing all tension along with exploration risk.
example: Space Invaders cannon width and bunkers. The hypothetical harder Kirby with a smaller inhale, one-hit deaths, no flight and more inertia. Kirby Super Star made standard enemies survive a few hits so stronger moves stood out.
review_question: Which specific dials set the risk in this game, and has each been set on purpose?
keywords: risk dials hitbox size health inertia game speed tuning parameters difficulty levers enemy hp target size

principle: Decide on purpose how much your game evens out skill
why: Competitive games are most fun when it's anyone's match. In casual games the most skilled player winning every time isn't fun, so catch-up systems are 'an absolute must', even if not quite fair. Smash wanted results to reflect skill, so it gives no stat help to trailing players and lets chaos (items, stages, Final Smashes) shake things up instead.
how_to_apply: Choose early: casual (everyone takes turns winning) or skill-reflecting. For casual play, give trailing players speed boosts or stronger items. For skill-reflecting play, leave core stats alone and route catch-up through chaos: make power-ups harder for the leader to get, charge comeback meters faster for losers. Keep variable-strength systems in party modes, out of level-playing-field matches. For home play, tolerate quirks players can house-rule.
anti_pattern: Letting the best player win every casual match; raising attack or reducing knockback for players who are behind in a skill game; stat-altering systems leaking into serious competition.
example: Mario Kart's boosts and items. Smash: the leader has a harder time getting a Smash Ball and the Final Smash Meter charges faster for losing players. Smash for 3DS/Wii U's variable character strength powered Smash Run, Smash Tour and amiibo.
review_question: How much does this game help the player who is behind, and was that a decision?
keywords: catch-up mechanics rubber banding comeback handicap party game competitive fairness skill gap items mario kart smash ball

principle: Never let luck alone decide a player's loss
why: Players need to feel, to some extent, that they are responsible for their own failure; losing only to bad luck is hard to accept and wastes hard work. Random dodge chances can feel unfair, and players already suspect computers of cheating with lucky rolls. Randomness still has value when using it well takes skill or when it gives anyone a shot at a comeback.
how_to_apply: Give players ways to respond to or control random events, keep randomness out of strict skill contests, prototype strategy combat without random evasion first, and keep random elements that still demand skill. Seed random numbers with an unpredictable value such as the system clock so resets can't force results.
anti_pattern: Matches decided by a single roll; leaning on a luck stat players forget; random rolls that swing the same battle unpredictably.
example: Peach's Smash Attack, once random, is now chosen with up or down. The Hero's randomized command list stays because each command takes skill. Wizardry's 1981 luck stat. Smash items stay random for comebacks.
review_question: Could a player lose this purely because of a random roll?
keywords: randomness rng luck fairness random evasion dice responsibility for failure seeding variance

principle: Let difficulty be a choice with stakes, not a humiliation
why: The Fiend's Cauldron let players bet hearts on higher Intensity for bigger rewards, and lowered difficulty automatically after failure, which stings less than asking whether you'd like to switch to Easy and means nobody plays the whole game on Easy. Xevious gave players a hidden lever: destroying one enemy rewinds the enemy table. Offering help is right, but do it without humiliating.
how_to_apply: Let players wager currency to raise difficulty for proportionally better rewards and pay to lower it; on failure, ease off automatically and take part of the stake. Give in-world levers that push difficulty back. If players can overpower themselves, treat it as a self-chosen difficulty and pay fewer rewards. Lock difficulty-lowering assists behind an unlock step so nobody flips them by accident.
anti_pattern: Bluntly asking failing players to switch to Easy; assists that can be switched on by accident; difficulty systems that never reward strong play.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron (default 2.0, 0.0 nearly invincible). Xevious's radar-station enemy. World of Light's Spirits. The Last of Us Part I's locked Combat Accessibility options.
review_question: Does lowering or raising difficulty feel like a decision the player owns?
keywords: difficulty wager fiend cauldron intensity dynamic difficulty adaptive assist mode self-chosen difficulty dignity stakes

principle: Check balance with testers and data, but let feel decide
why: Nobody is better at an in-development game than its play testers, and real match data shows whether every option has a shot: Smash Ultimate's 87 fighters fell between 47.18% and 51.43% win rate. But win rates aren't everything; the true metric is how each fighter feels. Identical setups should come out even, or the game isn't fair.
how_to_apply: Staff dedicated testers, use online and tournament results where you can, and test mirror matches for built-in side advantages. Look at multiplayer matches as well as top-tournament usage. Make final calls on feel, and step in as director mainly when an option's individuality is threatened.
anti_pattern: The director entering every parameter alone; judging fairness from one part of the game or from tournaments alone.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's win-rate spread. Brawl had only four testers and no online data. Rock, Paper, Scissors: identical teams draw.
review_question: What do your testers and data say, and does each option still feel right?
keywords: balance testing win rate data analytics playtesters tournament multiplayer mirror match fairness telemetry feel

principle: Make CPU opponents human-paced, aggressive and beatable
why: CPUs that react faster than a human feel extremely unfair, and players already suspect computers of cheating. Players who pick a high CPU level want a strong opponent, but one that waits around or perfect-shields everything would be invincible and no fun.
how_to_apply: Add a reaction delay, let status effects like reversed controls briefly confuse CPUs before they adapt, bias high levels toward offense, and cap perfect shields and dodges. Test for contradictions between AI behavior modes.
anti_pattern: Superhuman reaction speed; high-level CPUs that turtle or defend perfectly.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate CPUs have a 'reflex' and were tuned more aggressively than in past titles.
review_question: Could a human have reacted the way this CPU just did?
keywords: ai cpu opponents bots reaction time fairness difficulty levels aggression perfect shield computer players

principle: Show rank so most players feel they are succeeding
why: A leaderboard gives purpose, but for most players it means 'eternal humiliation': trying your hardest and landing 10,000th saps motivation, and seeing the gap to the world's best makes people give up. Matchmaking also has to balance finding a match against fair skill gaps.
how_to_apply: Show standing as a number that rises with skill, measured against the whole population. Hide the identity and score of the #1 player from general players. Give top players an elite tier that matches them with each other. Tune matchmaking range by region and time of day, widening only as needed.
anti_pattern: Raw position leaderboards for a huge player base; showing everyone their distance from the top; fixed matchmaking ranges.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Global Smash Power and Elite Smash.
review_question: What does the typical player see when they check their rank?
keywords: leaderboard ranking matchmaking elo mmr global smash power elite tier motivation online competitive

principle: Re-check difficulty after late performance changes, on real hardware
why: Meteos' speed was tied to processing speed, so a late optimization sped it up and made it harder than the per-planet tuning intended. Mushiking was tuned on a dev board and its Mushi got hungry faster on the production unit. Smash Ultimate's CPUs felt too hard at launch, possibly for a similar reason.
how_to_apply: Find any gameplay timing tied to processing speed, freeze it before final tuning, and replay difficulty-critical content after every optimization pass and on the actual retail hardware. Take it seriously when several people independently report the same feel problem.
anti_pattern: Tuning only on a dev kit; assuming smoother performance is purely a win when game speed tracks processing speed.
example: Meteos, Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking and Smash Bros. Ultimate.
review_question: Has the final difficulty been checked on the final build on real hardware?
keywords: performance optimization processing speed frame timing hardware testing difficulty regression late changes

principle: Check that co-op doesn't make the game harder than solo
why: In two-player Darius the ships get in each other's way and power-ups only cover one ship, which actually makes it harder; arcade Contra's two-player scroll point sits far forward. Kirby Super Star solved jump-heavy co-op by making one player the lead the camera follows.
how_to_apply: Playtest co-op for power-ups budgeted for one player, players blocking each other, and a camera or scroll point that strands the trailing player. Consider a lead-and-helper structure where an off-screen partner warps back.
anti_pattern: Dropping a second player into single-player resource and camera tuning unchanged.
example: Darius and Contra two-player modes; Kirby Super Star's Helper system.
review_question: Is the game easier or harder with a second player, and is that intended?
keywords: co-op multiplayer two player camera scrolling shared resources helper balance

principle: Give mismatched players handicap tools, and use them yourself
why: The skill gap between players can be painfully large. Settings can even it out, asymmetric fail conditions turn a mismatch into shared fun, and human adjustments, like letting a child grab the Smash Ball, may be the most effective handicap there is. Going easy isn't impolite unless the other person wants you to go all out.
how_to_apply: Expose difficulty and resources (lives, health, aggression) as separate per-player settings, offer asymmetric fail conditions, include an automatic handicap option, and ease off when you play newcomers.
anti_pattern: Framing every mismatched session as a strict winner-and-loser contest.
example: The Genji and the Heike Clans: hardest difficulty and fewest candles for Sakurai, easiest and most for Arino. Sakurai losing on one hit while Arino played to game over. Smash's automatic handicap setting.
review_question: Can a strong player and a weak player both enjoy the same session?
keywords: handicap per-player settings asymmetric fail condition mismatched skill family play going easy local multiplayer
